_note: Structured comparisons rendered by assets/js/explore.js, inside lessons and at #/compare. Each one is limited to services the current AZ-104 skills outline supports; objectives are verbatim bullets. Facts come from the Academy lessons (verified against Microsoft Learn) and from Microsoft Learn retrieved 2026-10-06.

excluded.title: NSG or Azure Firewall
excluded.reason: Azure Firewall is not in the AZ-104 skills measured or the study guide's documentation list.

comparisons.title: Microsoft Entra roles or Azure roles
comparisons.question: Does the task change the directory, or Azure resources?
objectives: Manage built-in Azure roles
Interpret access assignments

options.name: Microsoft Entra roles
options.purpose: Administer the directory: users, groups, licences, app registrations and tenant settings.
options.scope: The tenant, or narrower directory scopes such as an administrative unit.
options.when: Someone must create users, reset passwords, assign licences or change tenant settings.
options.difference: Grants nothing on Azure resources: a Global Administrator sees no VM until given an Azure role or elevating access.
options.limitation: Never assigned on a subscription or resource group.
options.dependency: A user or role-assignable group in the same tenant.
options.validate: Entra admin center: Roles & admins, the role, Assignments.

options.name: Azure roles (Azure RBAC)
options.purpose: Grant access to Azure resources: manage them (actions) or use their data (data actions).
options.scope: Management group, subscription, resource group or resource, inherited downward.
options.layer: Resource plane, enforced by Azure Resource Manager; data roles by the service.
options.when: Someone must create, change, view or use Azure resources or their data.
options.difference: Grants nothing in the directory: a subscription Owner can't create users.
options.limitation: Additive: NotActions removes permissions from one role, it doesn't deny what another assignment grants.
options.dependency: A principal from the tenant the subscription trusts, and a role definition.
options.validate: az role assignment list --assignee <upn> --all --include-inherited --include-groups, or IAM > Check access.

comparisons.takeaway: Directory task: Entra role. Resource task: Azure role. A scenario that needs both needs two assignments.

comparisons.title: Azure RBAC, Azure Policy or a resource lock
comparisons.question: Is the requirement about who may act, what may exist, or what must not change?
objectives: Implement and manage Azure Policy
Configure resource locks
Assign roles at different scopes

options.name: Azure RBAC
options.purpose: Decide who may perform which operations.
options.scope: Management group, subscription, resource group or resource.
options.when: The requirement names people, groups or apps and what they may do.
options.difference: About the caller; says nothing about how a resource must be configured.
options.limitation: Can't stop an authorized Owner from a mistaken delete.
options.dependency: Principals in the trusted tenant.
options.validate: Check access for the user; try the action as that user.

options.name: Azure Policy
options.purpose: Decide what may exist and how it must be configured, whoever deploys it.
options.scope: Usually a management group, subscription or resource group, with exclusions and exemptions below.
options.layer: Resource properties, evaluated by Resource Manager on create and update.
options.when: The requirement is about locations, SKUs, tags or settings.
options.difference: Deny blocks new or changed non-compliant resources; existing ones are only reported until remediated.
options.limitation: Remediation works only for modify and deployIfNotExists, through a remediation task with a managed identity.
options.dependency: A policy definition or initiative; a managed identity for remediation.
options.validate: Policy > Compliance, or az policy state summarize.

options.name: Resource lock
options.purpose: Stop deletion (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly), even by an Owner.
options.scope: Subscription, resource group or resource; not a management group.
options.when: Critical resources must not be deleted or changed by accident.
options.difference: Applies to everyone, including Owners, until someone removes the lock.
options.limitation: ReadOnly also blocks POST actions such as restarting a VM or listing storage keys; locks don't stop data-plane operations.
options.dependency: Permission on Microsoft.Authorization/locks (Owner or User Access Administrator) to create or remove it.
options.validate: az lock list --resource-group <rg>, then try the blocked action.

comparisons.takeaway: Who: RBAC. What may exist and how: Policy. Protect from deletion or change, even by admins: a lock.

comparisons.title: Availability set or availability zones
comparisons.question: Which failure must the VMs survive: a rack and maintenance, or a whole datacenter?
objectives: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets

options.name: Availability set
options.purpose: Spread VMs across fault domains (racks) and update domains (maintenance batches).
options.scope: One region, one datacenter.
options.layer: VM placement on hosts and racks.
options.when: The region has no zones, or you need rack-level separation within one datacenter.
options.difference: Protects against rack, host and planned-maintenance failures, not a datacenter outage.
options.limitation: A VM joins only at creation; up to 3 fault and 20 update domains; 99.95% SLA.
options.dependency: The set exists before or with the VMs.
options.validate: az vm get-instance-view shows each VM's platform fault and update domain.

options.name: Availability zones
options.purpose: Place VMs in separate datacenters within a region.
options.scope: One region with at least three zones.
options.layer: Datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking.
options.when: The workload must survive the loss of a zone.
options.difference: Survives a whole-zone outage.
options.limitation: Not every region or VM size supports zones; the zone is chosen at creation; 99.99% SLA with two or more VMs across zones.
options.dependency: Zone-aware dependencies, such as a zone-redundant Standard public IP or load balancer.
options.validate: az vm show --query zones.

comparisons.takeaway: Datacenter failure in scope: zones. Rack or maintenance only, or no zones in the region: availability set. Neither can be added to a VM that already exists.

comparisons.title: LRS, ZRS, GRS or GZRS
comparisons.question: How many copies, in how many places, and can the second region be read without a failover?
objectives: Configure Azure Storage redundancy

options.name: LRS
options.purpose: Three copies in one datacenter.
options.scope: Primary region, one datacenter.
options.when: Lowest cost, or data that can be re-created.
options.difference: No protection from a datacenter or zone outage.
options.limitation: A datacenter-level disaster can lose the data.
options.dependency: Nothing extra.
options.validate: az storage account show --query sku.name returns Standard_LRS.

options.name: ZRS
options.purpose: Three copies across three availability zones.
options.scope: Primary region only.
options.when: High availability inside one region, data kept in that region.
options.difference: Survives a zone outage; no copy outside the region.
options.limitation: The region must support zones; not every account type does.
options.dependency: A region with availability zones.
options.validate: sku.name returns Standard_ZRS.

options.name: GRS / RA-GRS
options.purpose: LRS in the primary region plus an asynchronous LRS copy in a secondary region.
options.scope: Primary and secondary (paired) region.
options.when: Survive a regional disaster; RA-GRS when apps must read the secondary without a failover.
options.difference: Secondary readable only with RA-, otherwise after a failover.
options.limitation: Asynchronous, so the newest writes can be lost; Premium accounts don't support it.
options.dependency: Azure chooses the secondary region.
options.validate: sku.name returns Standard_GRS or Standard_RAGRS.

options.name: GZRS / RA-GZRS
options.purpose: ZRS in the primary region plus an asynchronous copy in a secondary region.
options.scope: Primary and secondary region.
options.when: Zone resilience locally and protection from a regional disaster.
options.difference: The most resilient option.
options.limitation: Highest cost; availability varies by region and account type.
options.dependency: A primary region with zones.
options.validate: sku.name returns Standard_GZRS or Standard_RAGZRS.

comparisons.takeaway: Read the failure in scope: datacenter, ZRS; region, GRS or GZRS; must read during an outage without failing over, the RA- version.

comparisons.title: Managed disk, storage account data or temporary disk
comparisons.question: Is this a VM's drive, data shared over the network, or scratch space?
objectives: Manage virtual machine disks
Create and configure storage accounts

options.name: Managed disk
options.purpose: Persistent block storage attached to a VM: the OS disk and data disks.
options.scope: A resource in the VM's region (and zone).
options.when: A VM needs a drive that survives restarts and deallocation.
options.difference: Azure manages the storage behind it: you pick type and size, no storage account.
options.limitation: One VM at a time unless shared disks are used; type changes need the VM deallocated.
options.dependency: The VM it is attached to.
options.validate: az disk list --query "[].{name:name, sku:sku.name, state:diskState}" -o table.

options.name: Storage account data
options.purpose: Blobs, file shares, queues and tables reached over service endpoints.
options.scope: Containers and shares inside a storage account.
options.layer: Storage: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts and its data plane.
options.when: Data shared by many clients, apps or regions over HTTPS, SMB or NFS.
options.difference: Addressed by URL or share path, with its own firewall and authorization.
options.limitation: Name is globally unique, 3-24 lowercase letters and numbers; the account type can't change.
options.dependency: Network access and an authorization method.
options.validate: az storage account show; read or write a test object.

options.name: Temporary disk
options.purpose: Local scratch storage on the VM's host.
options.scope: The host running the VM.
options.when: Page or swap files and data you can afford to lose.
options.difference: Not persistent: data can be lost on maintenance, redeploy or deallocation.
options.limitation: Never keep data you need on it; some VM sizes have none.
options.dependency: The VM size.
options.validate: After a deallocate and start, the data is gone.

comparisons.takeaway: A VM drive that must persist: managed disk. Data shared over the network: storage account. Scratch only: temporary disk.

comparisons.title: Blob storage or Azure Files
comparisons.question: Do clients need objects by URL, or a mounted share with folders?
objectives: Create and configure a container in Azure Blob Storage
Create and configure a file share in Azure Files

options.name: Blob storage
options.purpose: Store objects of any type in containers, accessed over HTTPS.
options.scope: A container in a storage account.
options.when: Backups, logs, media, data lakes, static content.
options.difference: Objects addressed by URL; access tiers hot, cool, cold and archive.
options.limitation: Not a normal mounted drive; archived blobs need rehydration before they can be read.
options.dependency: A general-purpose v2 or premium block blob account.
options.validate: az storage blob list --container-name <c> --account-name <sa> --auth-mode login.

options.name: Azure Files
options.purpose: Managed file shares mounted over SMB or NFS.
options.scope: A share in a storage account.
options.when: Apps or users that expect a file share; lift-and-shift of file servers.
options.difference: Directories and files, share-level plus Windows ACL permissions, share snapshots.
options.limitation: SMB uses TCP port 445, which networks and ISPs often block.
options.dependency: A general-purpose v2 or premium file share account; an identity source for identity-based access.
options.validate: Mount the share from a VM and read and write a file.

comparisons.takeaway: URL access to objects: Blob. A mounted share with folders and ACLs: Azure Files.

comparisons.title: Service endpoint or private endpoint
comparisons.question: Must the PaaS resource get a private IP, or is it enough to allow certain subnets?
objectives: Configure service endpoints for Azure platform as a service (PaaS)
Configure private endpoints for Azure PaaS
Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks

options.name: Service endpoint
options.purpose: Send a subnet's traffic to a PaaS service over the Azure backbone with the subnet's identity, so the service firewall can allow it.
options.scope: Per subnet, per service (for example Microsoft.Storage).
options.layer: Routing and source identity; the service keeps its public endpoint.
options.when: Restrict a storage account to chosen subnets at no extra cost.
options.difference: The destination is still the service's public IP; DNS doesn't change.
options.limitation: Doesn't extend to on-premises; scoped to the service, not to one instance.
options.dependency: The endpoint on the subnet plus a virtual network rule on the resource.
options.validate: From the allowed subnet access works; from any other network it's refused.

options.name: Private endpoint
options.purpose: Give one PaaS resource a private IP inside your virtual network.
options.scope: A network interface in a subnet, mapped to one resource and sub-resource such as blob.
options.layer: A private IP plus DNS (a privatelink zone).
options.when: Private access from VNets, peered VNets or on-premises, with public access disabled.
options.difference: Traffic goes to a private IP in your address space.
options.limitation: Depends on DNS resolving the name to the private IP; billed hourly and per GB.
options.dependency: A subnet and a private DNS zone linked to the VNets that use it.
options.validate: nslookup <account>.blob.core.windows.net from inside the VNet returns a private IP.

comparisons.takeaway: Free, subnet-scoped, public IP unchanged: service endpoint. Private IP, reachable from on-premises, public access can be turned off: private endpoint.

comparisons.title: Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway
comparisons.question: Does the routing decision need to read HTTP?
objectives: Configure an internal or public load balancer
comparisons.note: Application Gateway isn't a skills-measured bullet. It appears in the study guide's documentation list and in Microsoft's AZ-104 networking learning path, so it's included only as the option to tell apart from Azure Load Balancer.

options.name: Azure Load Balancer
options.purpose: Distribute TCP and UDP flows across healthy backends.
options.scope: Regional; public or internal frontend.
options.when: Any TCP or UDP application, non-HTTP traffic, HA ports for appliances.
options.difference: Doesn't read HTTP: no URL routing, no TLS termination, no WAF.
options.limitation: Standard is closed to inbound traffic until an NSG allows it.
options.dependency: A backend pool in one VNet, a health probe, NSG rules allowing clients and 168.63.129.16.
options.validate: Data Path Availability and Health Probe Status metrics; connect to the frontend.

options.name: Application Gateway
options.purpose: Distribute HTTP and HTTPS requests with application-aware routing.
options.scope: Regional; public, private or both.
options.when: Route by URL path or host name, terminate TLS, or add a web application firewall.
options.difference: Terminates and reads HTTP, so /images and /api can go to different pools.
options.limitation: Needs a dedicated subnet; regional only.
options.dependency: A dedicated subnet, listeners, rules and backend pools.
options.validate: Its Backend health page; request each path and check which pool answers.

comparisons.takeaway: Ports and protocols: Load Balancer. URL paths, host names, TLS offload or WAF: Application Gateway.

comparisons.title: System-assigned or user-assigned managed identity
comparisons.question: Should the identity live and die with one resource, or be shared and managed on its own?
objectives: Create and manage an Azure Container Registry
Configure storage account encryption
comparisons.note: AZ-104 tests managed identities through the services that use them: pulling images from Container Registry (an ACI container group needs a user-assigned identity for this) and customer-managed keys for storage encryption.

options.name: System-assigned
options.purpose: An identity created on one resource and tied to it.
options.scope: Exactly one resource.
options.layer: A workload identity (service principal) in Microsoft Entra ID.
options.when: One resource needs its own access, removed when the resource is deleted.
options.difference: Deleted automatically with the resource.
options.limitation: Can't be shared, and can't be granted roles before the resource exists.
options.dependency: A resource type that supports managed identities.
options.validate: Resource > Identity shows Status On and an object ID; list its role assignments.

options.name: User-assigned
options.purpose: A standalone identity resource assigned to zero or more resources.
options.scope: Any resources you assign it to.
options.layer: A workload identity (service principal) in Microsoft Entra ID.
options.when: Several resources need the same access, access must exist before deployment, or resources are recreated often.
options.difference: Independent lifecycle: must be deleted explicitly.
options.limitation: Neither type removes its role assignments when deleted; clean them up.
options.dependency: The identity resource in a resource group.
options.validate: az identity show; az role assignment list --assignee <principalId> --all.

comparisons.takeaway: One resource, gone with it: system-assigned. Shared, created in advance, or surviving redeployments: user-assigned. Either way it needs a role assignment to do anything.

comparisons.title: Azure Monitor metrics or logs
comparisons.question: Do you need a number over time, or records you can search?
objectives: Interpret metrics in Azure Monitor
Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
Query and analyze logs in Azure Monitor

options.name: Metrics
options.purpose: Numeric values sampled over time.
options.scope: Per resource, split by dimensions.
options.when: Charts and near-real-time threshold alerts: CPU, transactions, availability.
options.difference: Platform metrics are collected automatically, with no setup.
options.limitation: Kept 93 days; numbers only, not who or why.
options.dependency: Nothing for platform metrics; the Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule for guest OS counters.
options.validate: Metrics explorer chart for the resource.

options.name: Logs
options.purpose: Records with many fields, queried with KQL.
options.scope: Tables in a Log Analytics workspace.
options.when: Investigations and audits: who changed what, which request failed.
options.difference: Resource logs exist only after you create a diagnostic setting.
options.limitation: Ingestion and retention are billed.
options.dependency: Diagnostic settings or agents with data collection rules, and a workspace.
options.validate: A KQL query returns recent rows, for example AzureActivity | take 10.

comparisons.takeaway: A threshold on a number: metric. Who, what and when: logs, and create the diagnostic setting first.

comparisons.title: Azure Backup or Azure Site Recovery
comparisons.question: Do you need the data as it was, or the workload running somewhere else?
objectives: Perform backup and restore operations by using Azure Backup
Configure Azure Site Recovery for Azure resources

options.name: Azure Backup
options.purpose: Keep point-in-time recovery points to restore data, files or whole VMs.
options.scope: Protected items in a Recovery Services vault or a Backup vault.
options.when: Recover from deletion, corruption or ransomware; restore an earlier version or one file.
options.difference: Goes back in time on a schedule set by the backup policy.
options.limitation: Changes after the latest recovery point aren't in it; restores take time.
options.dependency: A vault, a backup policy, the VM agent and extension.
options.validate: Backup items show a recent successful backup; do a test restore.

options.name: Azure Site Recovery
options.purpose: Replicate VMs continuously to another region and fail over.
options.scope: Replicated items in a Recovery Services vault.
options.when: Keep the workload running when its region is unavailable.
options.difference: Keeps a near-current replica and moves where the workload runs.
options.limitation: Recovery points are kept briefly (one day by default), so it isn't a backup; after failover you must reprotect.
options.dependency: A target region network, a cache storage account, the Mobility service extension.
options.validate: Replicated items are Healthy; a test failover into an isolated network succeeds.

comparisons.takeaway: Need the data as it was: Backup. Need the workload running in another region: Site Recovery. Many designs use both.

comparisons.title: ARM template or Bicep file
comparisons.question: Which language describes the deployment, and how do you move between them?
objectives: Interpret an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file

options.name: ARM template
options.purpose: Declare resources as JSON that Resource Manager deploys.
options.scope: Resource group, subscription, management group or tenant deployments.
options.when: Existing JSON templates, portal exports, tools that emit JSON.
options.difference: Verbose: bracket expressions, explicit dependsOn often needed.
options.limitation: Harder to read and change by hand.
options.dependency: A parameters file for per-environment values.
options.validate: what-if before deploying; the deployment's provisioningState is Succeeded.

options.name: Bicep
options.purpose: Declare the same resources in a simpler language.
options.scope: The same deployment scopes.
options.layer: Compiled to an ARM template before deployment.
options.when: New infrastructure as code; reuse with modules.
options.difference: Symbolic references create dependencies automatically; parent and existing keywords.
options.limitation: Decompiling JSON to Bicep is best-effort and can need clean-up.
options.dependency: The Bicep CLI: the Azure CLI installs it; Azure PowerShell needs it installed separately.
options.validate: az bicep build compiles cleanly; what-if before deploying.

comparisons.takeaway: Same engine, two languages. Read both; convert with az bicep decompile; export from the portal as either.
